I wake to the sound of rain arguing with the gutter. Not a clean, rhythmic rain, but the kind that hesitates, gathers, then throws itself down in sheets, as if the sky can't decide whether to apologize or rage. For a moment I lie still and let the house speak: the furnace clearing its throat, the refrigerator humming a note just under B-flat, the cat landing on the floor with a small thump like a dropped paperback. The clock says 6:47. Time has a texture at this hour, thick and granular, like sugar at the bottom of a coffee cup.

I have been asked to write a thousand words, whatever comes. The problem is that whatever comes always comes with baggage. It arrives wearing the scent of yesterday's bread, carrying a suitcase full of half-finished thoughts and the ghost of someone I used to be. Writing is not a faucet. It is more like standing in a river and trying to catch a particular current with your bare hands. You feel it moving past you all the time, but the moment you close your fingers, it changes shape.

So I write about the rain. I write about the cat, whose name is Moth, because when she was a kitten she kept flying into lampshades. She is now old and dignified and pretends she has never done anything foolish in her life, but I have seen her chase a sunbeam up a wall and lose. I write about the sound of tires on wet asphalt outside, the hiss that sounds like a secret being told to the street. I write about the blue-gray light that seeps through the curtains and turns the bedroom into a watercolor.

Memory is strange. It doesn't line up in chronological order; it pools. I can be standing at the sink, rinsing a mug, and suddenly I am eight years old, sitting on a porch step, watching my grandmother shell peas. The bowl was yellow plastic. The peas made a sound like tiny raindrops when they fell. I remember the way her hands moved, quick and certain, and how she hummed a song I never learned the name of. I remember thinking that being old must be like knowing all the songs. Now I am not old, but I am no longer eight, and I still don't know the song. Some things are lost not because we forget them, but because we never thought to ask.

The rain stops. A single bird begins to sing, a tentative, three-note phrase, as if testing the silence. Then another joins. Soon the whole block is a choir of invisible birds, and I think about how strange it is that we wake up and pretend the world is ordinary. It is not ordinary. It is a miracle that keeps insisting on itself: the way water falls from the sky, the way light bends, the way a heart keeps beating without being asked.

I pour coffee. The mug is blue, with a small chip on the rim. I like it because it is imperfect, and because it holds exactly the right amount of warmth. There is a comfort in small rituals. Making coffee, opening a window, watching the steam rise. These things anchor us. They are the stitches that hold the day together. Without them, time would unravel into a long, unmarked thread.

I think about the pressure to be productive. I think about how we have turned our days into lists, our hours into metrics. I think about how often I have mistaken busyness for meaning. But meaning is not in the number of words I write or the tasks I complete. It is in the quality of attention I bring to the moment. It is in noticing the way the light falls across the floor, the way the cat's whiskers twitch in a dream, the way the toast smells just before it burns. Attention is the rarest form of love, and we rarely offer it to the ordinary.

So I try to pay attention. I sit at the desk by the window. The wood is scratched from years of use. There is a coffee ring like a pale moon. I trace it with my finger. Outside, the street is dark with rain, and the trees are still dripping. A woman in a red coat walks by with a dog. The dog stops to sniff a patch of grass, and she waits, patient, looking at her phone. The whole scene lasts maybe twenty seconds, but it is a complete story: patience, distraction, a small creature following its nose.

I think about all the stories happening at once. In the apartment across the street, someone is making eggs. In another, someone is crying. Someone is laughing at a text. Someone is packing a bag. Someone is deciding whether to stay or leave. Every window is a lit rectangle of life, and I am just one of them. The idea should make me feel small, but instead it makes me feel connected. We are all in this together, this strange business of being alive.

The cat jumps onto the desk and settles into a loaf, her tail wrapped around her paws. She blinks at me slowly, which is cat for I love you, or maybe I tolerate you. I choose to believe it is love. I scratch behind her ears, and she purrs, a small engine of contentment. The sound is grounding. It reminds me that pleasure can be simple: a warm lap, a gentle hand, a quiet room.

The sun is beginning to break through now. The clouds are shifting from gray to silver to something almost gold. The light changes everything. The wet street glitters. The windows across the way turn to mirrors. The world, which a moment ago was soft and dim, becomes sharp and bright. It is a small resurrection, the kind that happens every day if we are awake to see it.

I think about what I am trying to say. Maybe I am trying to say that language is a net with holes too big to catch the river. Maybe I am trying to say that even so, we must keep casting. Because sometimes, for a moment, the water parts and we glimpse something: the exact shade of a rainy morning, the weight of a grandmother's hands, the way a cat's purr feels against the palm. And we think, yes, this is what it was like to be here.

The clock says 7:12. I have been sitting here for twenty-five minutes. I have written maybe eight hundred words. The rest will come or it won't. The rule was a thousand words, but the truth is no one is counting except the part of me that wants to do it right. I let that part sit in the corner and drink its tea. The rest of me watches the light move across the floor, slow as honey.

I remember a line from a poem I once read: "Let everything happen to you: beauty and terror. Just keep going. No feeling is final." I think about that. The rain, the cat, the coffee, the woman in the red coat, the grandmother shelling peas, the bird singing into the silence. All of it happened. All of it is happening still, somewhere, in the strange, layered present of memory. And I am here, holding it all in this small room, this small morning, trying to turn it into words.

The cat yawns. I yawn back. The rain begins again, gentle now, no longer arguing with the gutter but whispering to the leaves. The sound is soft, like pages turning. I close my eyes and listen. There is no rush. The day will unfold whether I hurry or not. The world will keep offering its small miracles. My only job is to notice.

Maybe that is the whole secret: to notice. To pay attention to the ordinary, fleeting, unrepeatable moments that make up a life. To let them touch you. To let them pass. And this one, like all the others, is already becoming memory.

I can be standing at the sink, rinsing a mug, and suddenly I am eight years old on a porch step, watching my grandmother shell peas. The bowl was yellow plastic. The peas made a sound like tiny raindrops. I remember her hands, quick and certain, and how she hummed a song I never learned the name of. I thought being old must be like knowing all the songs. Now I am not old, but I am no longer eight, and I still don't know the song. Some things are lost not because we forget them, but because we never thought to ask.

The rain stops. A bird sings a tentative three-note phrase, as if testing the silence. Soon the whole block is a choir of invisible birds, and I think how strange it is that we wake up and pretend the world is ordinary. It is not ordinary. It is a miracle that keeps insisting on itself: water falling from the sky, light bending, a heart beating without being asked.

I pour coffee. The mug is blue, with a small chip on the rim. I like it because it is imperfect and holds exactly the right amount of warmth. There is comfort in small rituals—making coffee, opening a window, watching steam rise. These things anchor us. They are the stitches that hold the day together. Without them, time would unravel into a long, unmarked thread.

I think about the pressure to be productive, how we have turned our days into lists and our hours into metrics, how often I have mistaken busyness for meaning. But meaning is not in the number of words I write or tasks I complete. It is in the quality of attention I bring to the moment: the light falling across the floor, the cat's whiskers twitching in a dream, the toast smelling just before it burns. Attention is the rarest form of love, and we rarely offer it to the ordinary.

So I try to pay attention. I sit by the window. The wood is scratched from years of use. There is a coffee ring like a pale moon. Outside, the street is dark with rain, and the trees are still dripping. A woman in a red coat walks by with a dog. The dog stops to sniff a patch of grass, and she waits, patient, looking at her phone. The whole scene lasts maybe twenty seconds, but it is a complete story: patience, distraction, a small creature following its nose.

I think about all the stories happening at once. In the apartment across the street, someone is making eggs. Someone is crying. Someone is laughing at a text. Someone is packing a bag. Someone is deciding whether to stay or leave. Every window is a lit rectangle of life, and I am just one of them. The idea should make me feel small, but instead it makes me feel connected. We are all in this strange business of being alive.

The cat jumps onto the desk and settles into a loaf, tail wrapped around her paws. She blinks at me slowly, which is cat for I love you, or maybe I tolerate you. I choose to believe it is love. I scratch behind her ears, and she purrs, a small engine of contentment. The sound is grounding. It reminds me that pleasure can be simple: a warm lap, a gentle hand, a quiet room.

The sun begins to break through. The clouds shift from gray to silver to something almost gold. The wet street glitters. The windows across the way turn to mirrors. The world, soft and dim a moment ago, becomes sharp and bright. It is a small resurrection, the kind that happens every day if we are awake to see it.

I think about what I am trying to say. Maybe I am trying to say that language is a net with holes too big to catch the river. Maybe I am trying to say that even so, we must keep casting. Because sometimes the water parts and we glimpse something: the exact shade of a rainy morning, the weight of a grandmother's hands, the way a cat's purr feels against the palm. And we think, yes, this is what it was like to be here.

The clock says 7:12. I have been sitting here for twenty-five minutes. I have written maybe eight hundred words. The rest will come or it won't. The rule was a thousand words, but the truth is no one is counting except the part of me that wants to do it right. I let that part sit in the corner and drink its tea. The rest of me watches the light move across the floor, slow as honey.

I remember a line from a poem: "Let everything happen to you: beauty and terror. Just keep going. No feeling is final." The rain, the cat, the coffee, the woman in the red coat, the grandmother shelling peas, the bird singing into the silence. All of it happened. All of it is happening still, somewhere, in the strange layered present of memory. And I am here, holding it all in this small room, this small morning, trying to turn it into words.

The cat yawns. I yawn back. The rain begins again, gentle now, no longer arguing with the gutter but whispering to the leaves. The sound is soft, like pages turning. I close my eyes and listen. There is no rush. The day will unfold whether I hurry or not. The world will keep offering its small miracles. My only job is to notice.

Maybe that is the whole secret: to notice. To pay attention to the ordinary, fleeting, unrepeatable moments that make up a life. To let them touch you. To let them pass. To write them down if you can, not to keep them, but to honor them. Because every moment is a once-in-a-lifetime event. No two rains are the same. No two cups of coffee. No two mornings. And this one, like all the others, is already becoming memory.

I wake to rain arguing with the gutter. Not clean rain but the kind that hesitates, gathers, then throws itself down as if the sky can't decide whether to apologize or rage. I lie still and let the house speak: the furnace clearing its throat, the refrigerator humming just under B-flat, the cat landing on the floor with a small thump. The clock says 6:47. I have been asked to write a thousand words, whatever comes. But whatever comes always comes with baggage. So I write about the rain. I write about the cat, whose name is Moth, because when she was a kitten she kept flying into lampshades. She is now old and dignified and pretends she has never done anything foolish, but I have seen her chase a sunbeam up a wall and lose. I write about the sound of tires on wet asphalt, the hiss like a secret being told to the street. I write about the blue-gray light that seeps through the curtains and turns the bedroom into a watercolor.

Memory is strange. It doesn't line up in chronological order; it pools. The peas made a sound like tiny raindrops. I remember her hands, quick and certain, and how she hummed a song I never learned the name of. I thought being old must be like knowing all the songs. Now I am not old, but I am no longer eight, and I still don't know the song. Some things are lost not because we forget them, but because we never thought to ask.

The rain stops. A bird sings a tentative three-note phrase, as if testing the silence. Soon the whole block is a choir of invisible birds, and I think how strange it is that we wake up and pretend the world is ordinary. It is not ordinary. It is a miracle that keeps insisting on itself: water falling from the sky, light bending, a heart beating without being asked.

I pour coffee. The mug is blue, with a small chip on the rim. I like it because it is imperfect and holds exactly the right amount of warmth. There is comfort in small rituals—making coffee, opening a window, watching steam rise. These things anchor us. They are the stitches that hold the day together. Without them, time would unravel into a long, unmarked thread.
